visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this chapter we look at the Indian countryside under Company rule, through the records that officials left behind. In this part we begin in Bengal with the Permanent Settlement and its effects. Then we turn to two peoples of the Rajmahal hills, the Paharias and the Santhals, and how the Company dealt with them.

slides.heading: The Permanent Settlement
slides.body_md: Introduced by **Lord Cornwallis** in **1793**; the revenue demand was **fixed in perpetuity**.

rows: Zamindars: rajas and taluqdars, recognised as owners of land
A regular revenue; investment in agriculture; a class of loyal landholders

visual.alt: Table, The Permanent Settlement. Who introduced it: Lord Cornwallis, Governor-General, in 1793; What was fixed: The revenue demand, in perpetuity; Who paid: Zamindars: rajas and taluqdars, recognised as owners of land; Aims: A regular revenue; investment in agriculture; a class of loyal landholders
visual.caption: The Permanent Settlement

slides.narration: In 1793 Lord Cornwallis, the Governor-General, introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal. The revenue demand was fixed for ever. The Company recognised zamindars, rajas and taluqdars, as owners of land responsible for paying the revenue. Its aims were a regular revenue, investment in agriculture, and a class of landholders loyal to the Company.

visual.caption: Who paid whom under the settlement

slides.narration: This diagram shows the flow of payment. The zamindar paid the fixed revenue to the Company, and it had to arrive before sunset on the due date. Below the zamindar were rich peasants and ryots who paid rent, and below them sharecroppers, who paid a share of the crop to those whose land they worked.

slides.heading: Zamindars under the new rules
slides.body_md: Owners of land, yet their **powers were curtailed**.

rows: Recognised as owners, but responsible for paying the revenue

visual.alt: Table, Zamindars under the new rules. Troops: Disbanded; Customs duties: Abolished; Courts: Placed under a Collector; Land and revenue: Recognised as owners, but responsible for paying the revenue
visual.caption: Zamindars under the new rules

slides.narration: The Company gave zamindars ownership but took away much of their authority. Their troops were disbanded, their customs duties were abolished, and their courts were placed under a Collector. They were now landholders who owed the Company a fixed sum, and no longer rulers of their estates in the old way.

slides.heading: Why zamindars defaulted
slides.body_md: A **high** demand, **low prices**, an **invariable** sum and the **sunset law**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Why zamindars defaulted: Demand set very high, then Low prices in the 1790s, then Same sum in every harvest, then Payment due by sunset, then Default and auction
visual.caption: Why zamindars defaulted

slides.narration: The demand was set very high. Prices of produce were low in the 1790s. The sum did not change whatever the harvest. And payment had to reach the Company by sunset on the due date, or the estate could be auctioned. Ryots also defaulted in bad years, so zamindars could not collect their rents. Many fell behind and lost estates.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a revenue ledger
slides.body_md: Imagined estate, fixed demand **500** a year; collections **540, 450, 520**.
bullets: Step 1 — Compare each year with the **demand**.
Step 2 — Find the **total** collected and compare.

visual.caption: Reading a revenue ledger

slides.narration: Take an imagined estate with a fixed demand of five hundred. Collections are five forty, four fifty and five twenty. The total is fifteen hundred and ten, ten above the demand. Yet in year two the estate was fifty short. Because payment was due each year, a good total can hide a bad year that ruins an estate.

slides.heading: Auctions and the zamindars' answers
slides.body_md: In **1797** much of the **Burdwan** raj's estates was auctioned; zamindars found ways to keep control.

rows: A sale in a false name; the zamindar kept control
Estates put in their names; the Company did not take women's property
Agents bought at auction for the old owner

visual.alt: Table, Zamindars' answers to auctions. Benami sale: A sale in a false name; the zamindar kept control; Women of the family: Estates put in their names; the Company did not take women's property; Buying back through agents: Agents bought at auction for the old owner; Lathyals: Strongmen kept outside buyers away
visual.caption: Zamindars' answers to auctions

slides.narration: Estates were auctioned, and in 1797 a large part of the Burdwan raj was sold. Zamindars used tricks. They made benami sales in false names, put estates in the names of women of the family, whose property the Company did not take over, bought estates back through agents, and used lathyals, strongmen, to keep outside buyers away.

slides.heading: Jotedars
slides.body_md: Rich peasants who held **large areas** and often **overshadowed the zamindars**.

rows: Rich peasants, notably in north Bengal, as in Dinajpur
Large areas, sometimes thousands of acres
Trade, moneylending and village influence; zamindars based in towns
Often resisted zamindars; some bought estates at auction

visual.alt: Table, Jotedars. Who: Rich peasants, notably in north Bengal, as in Dinajpur; Land: Large areas, sometimes thousands of acres; Labour: Sharecroppers called adhiyars or bargadars; Power: Trade, moneylending and village influence; zamindars based in towns; Relation: Often resisted zamindars; some bought estates at auction
visual.caption: Jotedars

slides.narration: Jotedars were rich peasants, especially in north Bengal, as in Dinajpur. They held large areas, sometimes thousands of acres, controlled local trade and moneylending, and had sharecroppers cultivate their land. They lived in the villages, while zamindars were based in towns, so jotedars were often more powerful locally and resisted zamindars. Some even bought estates at auction.

slides.heading: The Paharias
slides.body_md: People of the **Rajmahal hills** who lived by **forest produce** and **shifting cultivation**.

headers: The Paharias of the Rajmahal hills
rows: Hunting; forest produce such as mahua flowers, silk cocoons and resin
Shifting cultivation: patches cleared by burning, pulses and millets sown with a hoe
Raids on settlements, a way of claiming a share and asserting control

visual.alt: Table, The Paharias. Livelihood: Hunting; forest produce such as mahua flowers, silk cocoons and resin; Farming: Shifting cultivation: patches cleared by burning, pulses and millets sown with a hoe; The forest: Central to their identity; Plains: Raids on settlements, a way of claiming a share and asserting control
visual.caption: The Paharias

slides.narration: The Paharias lived around the Rajmahal hills, in present day Jharkhand. They hunted and gathered forest produce such as mahua flowers, silk cocoons and resin. They also practised shifting cultivation, clearing patches by burning and sowing pulses and millets with a hoe. The forest was central to their identity. They also raided plains settlements, as a way of claiming a share and asserting control.

slides.heading: The Company and the Paharias
slides.body_md: From **extermination** to **pacification**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, The Company and the Paharias: 1770s: a policy of brutal extermination, then 1780s: Cleveland's pacification, then Allowances paid to chiefs, then Chiefs lose standing; Paharias retreat
visual.caption: The Company and the Paharias

slides.narration: In the 1770s the Company followed a policy of brutal extermination. In the 1780s Augustus Cleveland, Collector of Bhagalpur, tried pacification instead. Chiefs were given annual allowances to ensure the good conduct of their men. Many chiefs who accepted lost standing among their own people, and the Paharias withdrew deeper into the hills.

slides.heading: The Santhals and the Damin-i-Koh
slides.body_md: Settled cultivators who cleared forest; **1832**: the **Damin-i-Koh**.

rows: Santhals arrive as settled cultivators, clearing forest with the Company's encouragement
A large area marked out as the Damin-i-Koh, the land of the Santhals
Settlements spread rapidly; the Paharias are pushed deeper into the hills

visual.alt: Table, The Santhals and the Damin-i-Koh. From the 1780s: Santhals arrive as settled cultivators, clearing forest with the Company's encouragement; 1832: A large area marked out as the Damin-i-Koh, the land of the Santhals; After 1832: Settlements spread rapidly; the Paharias are pushed deeper into the hills
visual.caption: The Santhals and the Damin-i-Koh

slides.narration: From about the 1780s the Santhals came into the region as settled cultivators, clearing forests with the encouragement of the Company. In 1832 a large area was marked out as the Damin i Koh, declared to be the land of the Santhals. Their settlements spread rapidly, and the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills.

slides.heading: The hul
slides.body_md: Heavy tax, **dikus** and zamindars; the rising of **1855 to 1856**.

rows: Heavy state tax; moneylenders (dikus) and loss of land; zamindars' claims on the Damin area
Santhal Pargana created in 1856 with special laws to conciliate the Santhals

visual.alt: Table, The hul. Grievances: Heavy state tax; moneylenders (dikus) and loss of land; zamindars' claims on the Damin area; Leaders: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu; Rising: The hul of 1855 to 1856, suppressed; Afterwards: Santhal Pargana created in 1856 with special laws to conciliate the Santhals
visual.caption: The hul

slides.narration: The Santhals found that the land they had cleared was heavily taxed. Moneylenders, whom they called dikus, charged high interest and took their land when they could not repay, and zamindars claimed control over the Damin area. In 1855 to 1856 Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the hul, which was suppressed. Afterwards the Santhal Pargana was created in 1856, with special laws.

goals: Explain the ryotwari system and why Deccan ryots fell into debt
Explain the cotton boom, its end in 1865 and the use of bonds under the law of 1859

slides.heading: The Deccan and Official Archives
slides.body_md: Part 2: **ryotwari**, **cotton**, the **riots of 1875** and **official reports**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Part 2 at a glance: Ryotwari in the Deccan, then Cotton boom and bust, then The riots of 1875, then Reading official reports
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we move to the Bombay Deccan. We study the ryotwari system, the cotton boom and the debt that followed, and the riots of 1875. Then we ask how historians read the official reports of the period, the Fifth Report, Buchanan journals and the Deccan Riots Commission.

slides.heading: The ryotwari system
slides.body_md: Revenue settled with the **ryot**, assessed on soil, revised every **30 years**.

rows: The ryot, the cultivator himself, not a zamindar
Based on expected average income from different types of soil
Every 30 years, at a high level
Many ryots fled or fell into debt in the depression of the 1830s

visual.caption: The ryotwari system

slides.narration: In the 1820s the ryotwari system was introduced in the Bombay Deccan. Revenue was settled directly with the ryot, the cultivator, and not through a zamindar. It was based on the expected average income from different types of soil, and revised every thirty years, at a high level. Many ryots fled or fell into debt in the depression of the 1830s.

slides.heading: Why ryots turned to moneylenders
slides.body_md: A high assessment, bad years, **flight and debt**.

nodes.label: High assessment fixed for long periods

visual.alt: Flow chart, Why ryots turned to moneylenders: High assessment fixed for long periods, then Bad years and low incomes, then Ryots flee or borrow, then Dependence on moneylenders grows
visual.caption: Why ryots turned to moneylenders

slides.narration: An assessment fixed at a high level for long periods left ryots little to spare. In bad years, such as the depression of the 1830s, many fled or fell into debt. They turned to moneylenders, called sahukars, and so their dependence on moneylenders grew. This was the setting for the later troubles of the Deccan.

slides.heading: The cotton boom
slides.body_md: The **American Civil War**, 1861 to 1865, cut off cotton from the USA.

nodes.label: British mills lose cotton from the USA
Demand for Indian cotton and prices rise
Cotton spreads in the Bombay Deccan

visual.caption: The cotton boom

slides.narration: British cotton interests, such as the Cotton Supply Association of 1857 and the Manchester Cotton Company of 1859, had already looked to India. When the American Civil War from 1861 to 1865 cut off raw cotton from the United States, demand for Indian cotton rose sharply, and cotton cultivation expanded in the Bombay Deccan.

slides.body_md: Why did demand for Deccan cotton rise in the early 1860s?

slides.heading: The chain of credit
slides.body_md: **Exporters**, then **sahukars**, then **ryots**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, The chain of credit: Exporters advance money, then Sahukars lend to ryots, then Ryots expand cotton, then Prices soar
visual.caption: The chain of credit

slides.narration: Money moved down a chain. Exporters advanced money to sahukars, and sahukars lent to ryots so that they could grow more cotton. Prices soared and credit flowed easily. Ryots took loans on the expectation that the good prices would last. The chain would soon work in the opposite direction.

slides.heading: The Limitation Law and the bonds
slides.body_md: A bond valid for only **three years**; new bonds with **interest added**.

slides.narration: The Limitation Law of 1859 said that a loan bond was valid for only three years. So moneylenders made ryots sign new bonds every three years, often adding the unpaid interest to the principal. They also used other tricks, such as not giving receipts, entering fictitious figures, and taking over produce at low prices.

slides.heading: After 1865
slides.body_md: American cotton returned; **demand fell** and **credit dried up**.

nodes.label: Credit dries up; ryots in debt

visual.alt: Flow chart, The bust: War ends in 1865, then American cotton returns, then Demand for Indian cotton falls, then Credit dries up; ryots in debt
visual.caption: The bust

slides.narration: When the American war ended in 1865, American cotton returned to British mills. Demand for Indian cotton fell, and credit dried up. Ryots who had borrowed during the boom were left with debts. Under the Limitation Law practice, those debts grew with each new bond, while the price of their crop no longer helped them.

slides.body_md: May 1875, **Supa**: ryots attacked **sahukars** and burnt their **bonds**.

Ryots attacked sahukars, moneylenders and traders, demanded their bonds and account books, called bahi khatas, and burnt them. The revolt spread to villages in Poona and Ahmednagar districts. slides.body_md: Set up by the **Government of Bombay**; report to **Parliament**, **1878**.

rows: Presented to the British Parliament in 1878
Statements of ryots, sahukars and eyewitnesses; statistics on revenue rates, prices and interest

visual.caption: The Deccan Riots Commission

slides.narration: The Government of Bombay set up the Deccan Riots Commission to inquire into the riots. Its report was presented to the British Parliament in 1878. It collected statements from ryots, sahukars and eyewitnesses, and statistics on revenue rates, prices and interest. It concluded that the anger was against moneylenders and grain dealers, and was reluctant to accept the revenue demand as a cause.

slides.heading: Reading official reports
slides.body_md: Ask **who**, **for whom**, **what** and **what is missing**.

visual.alt: Table, Questions for an official report. Who wrote it?: Position shapes viewpoint; For whom, and why?: Purpose shapes what is recorded; What does it record?: The evidence it offers; What does it leave out?: Silences and missing voices
visual.caption: Questions for an official report

slides.narration: Official reports are valuable, but they were written with particular purposes and viewpoints. Historians read them for what they record, and question what they leave out and how they explain events. So we ask four things: who wrote it, for whom and why, what it records, and what it leaves out.

slides.body_md: A report to **Parliament** in **1813**, with long **appendices**.

slides.narration: The Fifth Report of 1813 was a report on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India, submitted to the British Parliament. It had about a thousand pages, over eight hundred of them appendices of petitions, collectors reports and revenue statistics. It shaped British understanding of rural Bengal, but it was written to criticise the Company, so it may exaggerate the decline of zamindari power.

sections.heading: 1. The Permanent Settlement of 1793
sections.body_md:
In **1793** **Lord Cornwallis**, the Governor-General, introduced the **Permanent Settlement** in Bengal. The revenue demand was fixed **in perpetuity**. The Company recognised **zamindars** (rajas and taluqdars) as owners of land and responsible for paying the revenue. Its aims were a **regular revenue**, **investment in agriculture** and a class of **loyal landholders**.

The Company also curtailed the zamindars' powers: their **troops were disbanded**, their **customs duties were abolished** and their **courts were placed under a Collector**. Zamindars were now landholders who owed a fixed sum, not local rulers in the old way.

A landholder (raja or taluqdar) recognised as owner and responsible for paying the revenue.

sections.heading: 2. Auctions, tricks and the jotedars
sections.body_md:
Many zamindars **defaulted**. The demand was fixed **very high**; **prices of produce were low** in the 1790s; the sum was **invariable**, the same in every harvest; and the **sunset law** required payment to reach the Company by sunset on the due date, or the estate could be **auctioned**. Ryots also defaulted in bad years, so zamindars could not collect rents. In **1797** a large part of the **Burdwan** raj's estates was auctioned.

Zamindars answered with tricks: **benami** (fictitious) sales; putting estates in the names of **women of the family**, since the Company did not take over women's property; **buying back through agents**; and **lathyals** (strongmen) to keep outside buyers away.

**Jotedars** were rich peasants, especially in north Bengal, as in **Dinajpur**. They held large areas, sometimes thousands of acres, controlled local trade and moneylending, and had land cultivated by sharecroppers (**adhiyars** or **bargadars**). They lived in villages, while zamindars were based in towns, so jotedars were often more powerful locally and resisted zamindars. Some bought estates at auction.

A rich peasant of north Bengal with large holdings, trade, moneylending and sharecroppers.

sections.heading: 3. The Paharias
sections.body_md:
The **Paharias** lived around the **Rajmahal hills**, in present-day Jharkhand. They **hunted**, gathered **forest produce** (mahua flowers, silk cocoons, resin) and practised **shifting cultivation**, clearing patches by burning and sowing pulses and millets with a hoe. The forest was central to their identity. They also raided plains settlements, as a way of claiming a share of the produce and asserting control.

In the **1770s** the Company followed a policy of brutal extermination. In the **1780s** **Augustus Cleveland**, Collector of Bhagalpur, introduced **pacification**: chiefs were given annual allowances to ensure the good conduct of their men. Many chiefs who accepted lost standing among their people, and the Paharias withdrew deeper into the hills.

**Francis Buchanan**, a physician, toured the region for the Company in 1810–11 and recorded his observations in journals. He saw the land through the Company's eyes, as resources to be developed, and was critical of the forest dwellers' ways. Officials' views of the Paharias are the officials' views, to be set beside evidence of their own way of life.

sections.heading: 4. The Santhals and the hul
sections.body_md:
From about the **1780s** the **Santhals** came into the region as **settled cultivators**, clearing forest with the Company's encouragement. In **1832** a large area was marked out as the **Damin-i-Koh**, declared the land of the Santhals. Their settlements spread rapidly, and the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills.

The Santhals found that the land they had cleared was **heavily taxed**; **moneylenders** (**dikus**) charged high interest and took their land when they could not repay; and **zamindars** claimed control over the Damin area. In **1855–56** the Santhals rose in the **hul**, led by **Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu**. The rising was suppressed, and in **1856** the **Santhal Pargana** was created, with special laws meant to conciliate them.

sections.heading: 5. Ryotwari, cotton and the cycle of debt
sections.body_md:
The **ryotwari system** was introduced in the Bombay Deccan in the **1820s**. Revenue was settled directly with the **ryot**, not through a zamindar. The assessment was based on the **expected average income** from different types of soil and was **revised every 30 years**, at a high level. Many ryots fled or fell into debt in the depression of the **1830s**.

British cotton interests, the **Cotton Supply Association** (1857) and the **Manchester Cotton Company** (1859), had already sought supplies from India. The **American Civil War** (1861–65) cut off raw cotton from the USA, demand for Indian cotton soared and cotton cultivation expanded in the Deccan. Exporters advanced money to **sahukars**, who lent to ryots. When the war ended in **1865**, American cotton returned, demand fell and credit dried up, leaving ryots in debt.

The **Limitation Law of 1859** gave loan bonds validity for only **three years**, so moneylenders made ryots sign **new bonds** every three years, often adding unpaid interest to the principal; they also gave no receipts, entered fictitious figures and took over produce at low prices.

sections.heading: 6. The riots of 1875 and the Deccan Riots Commission
sections.body_md:
The **Deccan riots** began in **May 1875** at **Supa**, a large village in Poona district. Ryots attacked sahukars, demanded their **bonds** and **account books** (bahi khatas) and **burnt** them. The revolt spread to villages in Poona and Ahmednagar districts. Police were posted in villages and many people were arrested.

The **Government of Bombay** set up the **Deccan Riots Commission**. Its report was presented to the British Parliament in **1878**. It collected statements from ryots, sahukars and eyewitnesses and statistics on revenue rates, prices and interest. It concluded that the anger was against **moneylenders and grain dealers**, and it was reluctant to accept that the government's revenue demand was a cause. Historians note that such a report must be read with care on that point.

sections.heading: 7. Official archives as sources
sections.body_md:
The **Fifth Report** (1813) was a report on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India, submitted to the **British Parliament**; it was the fifth of a series. It had about **1,002 pages**, over **800** of them appendices of petitions, collectors' reports and revenue statistics. It shaped British understanding of rural Bengal, but historians note that it was written to **criticise the Company's mismanagement**, so it may have exaggerated the decline of zamindari power.

**Buchanan's journals** (1810–11) and the **Deccan Riots Commission report** (1878) are also official sources. Each was written with a particular **purpose** and **viewpoint**. Historians read them for what they record and question **what they leave out** and **how they explain events**, testing them against other evidence such as petitions, registers and the people's own accounts.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the Settlement's demand was revised with harvests; it was fixed.
- Calling zamindars cultivators; they were recognised owners paying the revenue.
- Describing Paharia raids only as plunder; say officials saw it so, and that it was also a claim to a share.
- Presenting an officer's view of a people as the truth about them.
- Counting simple interest when bonds added unpaid interest to the principal.
- Saying the Commission proved the revenue demand had no part; it was reluctant to accept it.
- Treating official reports as neutral and complete.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points, or a point and a reason (30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five headed points (80–120 words); assess questions need more than one side and a judgement.
- Source questions (4 marks): parts (a) and (b) one mark each, part (c) two marks with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, and in which year?

options.text_md: Warren Hastings, in 1772
Lord Cornwallis, in 1793
Lord Wellesley, in 1798
Lord Dalhousie, in 1856

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Lord Cornwallis, in 1793. Cornwallis was Governor-General when the revenue demand was fixed for ever. The other pairs name different officials and years.

questions.stem_md: Which of these was NOT among the aims with which the Company introduced the Permanent Settlement?

options.text_md: To secure a regular flow of revenue
To encourage landholders to invest in agriculture
To create a class of landholders loyal to the Company
To raise the revenue demand each year as the price of grain rose

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To raise the revenue demand each year as the price of grain rose. A demand fixed in perpetuity could not be raised with prices; that is the opposite of the plan. The other three were stated aims.

questions.stem_md: Some historians say that the low prices of agricultural produce in the 1790s helped to push zamindars into default. Which finding about an imagined district would most weaken this explanation for that district?

options.text_md: Records showing that produce prices there stayed high throughout the 1790s, yet its estates were auctioned as often as estates elsewhere
Records showing that prices there fell sharply in the early 1790s and that auctions rose soon after
A zamindar's petition saying that low prices made it hard to find the sum due
Records showing that ryots paid less rent in the years when prices were low

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Records showing that produce prices there stayed high throughout the 1790s, yet its estates were auctioned as often as estates elsewhere. To weaken a cause, look for the effect appearing without it. The other findings fit the explanation or support it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated letter from a district Collector says that zamindars of his district are asking to have their estates entered in the names of women of their families, reports that a large part of the Burdwan raj's estates has been sold at auction, and calls the revenue arrangement a recent measure. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: Before 1793, since zamindars were already anxious about the revenue
About 1857, since auctions of estates were common then
Not before 1797, and probably within a few years of it, since the arrangement is called recent
It cannot be dated, since the letter gives no year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Not before 1797, and probably within a few years of it, since the arrangement is called recent. The auction of Burdwan lands sets an earliest date, and the word recent narrows the range. A letter can often be dated from what it reports even when it gives no year.

questions.stem_md: An imagined auction record shows that an estate was bought by a man named Ramtanu, who paid the full price within a week and has no earlier record of owning land. Which further record would best show whether the sale was benami, that is, made in a false name on behalf of the former zamindar?

options.text_md: The revenue demand fixed on the district for the year of the sale
A list of the other estates sold in the same district that year
Rent receipts after the sale showing that the estate's villages still paid the former zamindar's treasurer
A record of the price of rice in the district in the year of the sale

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rent receipts after the sale showing that the estate's villages still paid the former zamindar's treasurer. A benami buyer holds the estate in name only, so the test is whether the real control and income stayed with the old owner. The other records do not bear on who controlled the estate.

questions.stem_md: Historians say that jotedars were often more powerful in north Bengal villages than the zamindars. Which finding about an imagined village would most weaken this claim for that village?

options.text_md: Records showing that the zamindar's agents controlled the village's grain trade and lending, and that the jotedar paid whatever rent they fixed each year
Records showing a jotedar with hundreds of acres cultivated by sharecroppers
A record of a jotedar refusing to pay rent to the zamindar's agents
A record of villagers borrowing grain from a jotedar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Records showing that the zamindar's agents controlled the village's grain trade and lending, and that the jotedar paid whatever rent they fixed each year. The claim concerns who held power in the village. Only the first finding shows the zamindar's side in command; the others describe the jotedar's strength.

questions.stem_md: An imagined zamindar must pay a fixed 600 rupees a year, whatever the harvest. From his ryots he collects 720, 610, 480 and 650 rupees in four successive years. Which statement follows from these figures?

options.text_md: He was never at risk, because his four-year total was above the total demand
He was short of the demand in two of the four years
His shortfall in the third year was 60 rupees, the same as his surplus over the four years
His four-year collections exceeded the demand by 60 rupees, but in the third year he was 120 rupees short, so one bad year could still endanger the estate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** His four-year collections exceeded the demand by 60 rupees, but in the third year he was 120 rupees short, so one bad year could still endanger the estate. The four years bring in 2,460 rupees against a demand of 2,400, a surplus of 60. In the third year 480 falls 120 below 600. Payment was due in each year, so a surplus elsewhere could not cover it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After 1793 the Company disbanded the zamindars' troops, abolished their customs duties and placed their courts under a Collector.

**Reason (R):** The Company fixed the revenue demand in perpetuity.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because the revenue demand of the Permanent Settlement was fixed in perpetuity, the Company lowered it in years of poor harvest.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The demand did not change with the harvest, which is exactly what made bad years dangerous for zamindars.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the Company cut down the powers of zamindars after the Permanent Settlement.
questions.solution_md: Two of the three curbs named, with their effect.

answer.model_answer_md: The Company **disbanded the zamindars' troops** and **abolished the customs duties** they had collected. Their **courts were placed under a Collector**, so they could no longer act as rulers of their estates; they were treated as landholders who owed the Company revenue.

questions.stem_md: In one imagined district 40 of 100 estates were auctioned between 1793 and 1805; in a neighbouring district with the same revenue demand per acre only 10 of 100 were. Suggest two explanations, other than carelessness, for the difference.
questions.solution_md: Two rival explanations, one from conditions and one from evasion.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Harvests or prices** may have been worse in the first district, so rents fell short while the demand stayed fixed. (2) Zamindars of the second may have used **benami sales or women's names** to keep estates, so fewer auctions appear in the records.

marking_scheme.step: An explanation from harvests or prices
An explanation from evasion of auctions

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why jotedars of north Bengal were often more powerful in the villages than the zamindars.
questions.solution_md: Residence and landholding, then control of trade and credit.

answer.model_answer_md: Jotedars **lived in the villages** and held large areas, sometimes thousands of acres, while the zamindar's base lay in the towns. They also **controlled local trade and moneylending**, and sharecroppers worked their land, so villagers depended on them.

marking_scheme.step: Lived in villages with large holdings, unlike the town-based zamindar
Control of trade and moneylending, with sharecroppers

questions.stem_md: In an imagined year the harvest fails on an estate and its ryots pay only half their rent, but the zamindar's revenue is due on a fixed date. Name two courses open to him and one risk of each.
questions.solution_md: Two practical courses taken from the period, each with its risk.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) He could **borrow** to pay on time; the risk is a **debt** he cannot repay after another poor year. (2) He could **enter the estate in a woman's name** or use a benami buyer to protect it; the risk is that the Collector may see through the device.

marking_scheme.step: A second course with its risk

questions.stem_md: Explain three reasons why many zamindars found it hard to pay the revenue fixed under the Permanent Settlement.
questions.solution_md: Three causes of default drawn from the terms of the settlement and the conditions of the 1790s.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The demand was set at a **very high level**. (2) **Prices of produce were low** in the 1790s, so rents from ryots bought little. (3) The sum was **invariable**, the same in good and bad harvests, and had to reach the Company by sunset on the due date. Ryots' own defaults made rents harder to collect.

marking_scheme.step: Invariable sum with a strict date

questions.stem_md: In an imagined year of failed harvest in north Bengal, a zamindar based in a town and a jotedar living in a village both lose income. Give three reasons why the jotedar was probably better placed to cope.
questions.solution_md: Three advantages of the jotedar, each set against the zamindar's position.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The zamindar owed a **fixed revenue** by a fixed date whatever the harvest, so he risked auction. (2) The jotedar **controlled local trade and moneylending**, so he could buy grain and lend to needy villagers. (3) He **lived in the village** and had sharecroppers on his land, while the zamindar's base lay in the town. These are likely advantages, not certainties.

marking_scheme.step: Presence in the village and sharecroppers

questions.stem_md: Describe the Permanent Settlement of 1793 and explain why it brought difficulties for many zamindars.
questions.solution_md: The settlement and its terms, the aims, the curbs on power and the causes of default.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Introduction:** Lord Cornwallis, the Governor-General, introduced it in Bengal in 1793; the revenue demand was fixed in perpetuity.
2. **Zamindars:** the Company recognised rajas and taluqdars as zamindars, owners of the land and responsible for paying the revenue.
3. **Aims:** a regular revenue, investment in agriculture and a class of loyal landholders.
4. **Limits on power:** troops were disbanded, customs abolished and courts placed under a Collector.
5. **Difficulties:** the demand was high, prices were low in the 1790s, the sum did not change with harvests and payment was due by sunset; many defaulted and estates, such as much of Burdwan's in 1797, were auctioned.

marking_scheme.step: Introduction in 1793 and the fixed demand
Zamindars recognised as owners paying revenue

questions.stem_md: An imagined historian says that the Permanent Settlement failed in its own aims. Assess this claim, using the aims, the difficulties of the zamindars and the position of the jotedars.
questions.solution_md: The aims set against evidence on both sides, then a measured verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Aims:** a regular revenue, investment in agriculture and a class of loyal landholders.
2. **For the claim:** a high demand, low prices and the sunset rule led to defaults and auctions, so the Company's chosen landholders were often removed.
3. **Against:** zamindars used benami sales, women's names and lathyals to keep estates, so auctions did not always change who held them.
4. **Jotedars:** rich peasants held real power in villages and often resisted zamindars.
5. **Judgement:** a fixed demand did give the Company a predictable sum, so the first aim was partly met; but the loyal class was shaky and nothing above shows investment. So failed is too strong; only partly achieved is safer.

questions.stem_md: Company records of the late eighteenth century describe the Paharias as living around which hills?

options.text_md: The Aravalli hills
The Rajmahal hills
The Nilgiri hills
The Vindhya hills

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Rajmahal hills. The Rajmahal hills lie in present-day Jharkhand; the others are far from the region of these records.

questions.stem_md: Company officials called the Paharias' raids on plains villages plunder. A historian suggests that the raids were also a way of claiming a share of the plains produce and asserting control. Which finding about an imagined Paharia group would most strengthen her suggestion?

Her suggestion is that raids were a claim to a share. A claim is met when the share is paid, so the raids ending after regular payment supports it; the other findings say nothing about a claim.

questions.stem_md: In the 1780s the Collector Augustus Cleveland paid annual allowances to Paharia chiefs so that they would keep their men in good conduct. Which finding about the years that followed would most weaken the view that the allowances kept the peace?

Records showing that some chiefs lost standing among their own people

questions.stem_md: A student writes that Francis Buchanan's journals of 1810–11 prove that Paharia shifting cultivation was wasteful. What is the soundest response?

The journals can be ignored, since a physician knew nothing of farming
The journals show how a physician working for the Company judged the land, as resources to be developed, so the claim must be checked against evidence of how the Paharias used it
The claim is sound, since official journals are neutral

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The journals show how a physician working for the Company judged the land, as resources to be developed, so the claim must be checked against evidence of how the Paharias used it. A journal is evidence of its writer's view, and this writer's view was shaped by the Company's interest. It is neither proof nor worthless.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated letter from a district officer says that Santhal villages have multiplied inside the area marked out for them, that moneylenders are pressing them hard, that two brothers named Sidhu and Kanhu are said to be moving from village to village, and that no uprising has yet begun. answer.model_answer_md: The Paharias lived by **hunting and gathering forest produce** such as mahua flowers, silk cocoons and resin, and by **shifting cultivation**: they cleared patches by burning and sowed pulses and millets with a hoe. The forest was central to their identity.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Company officer writes that shifting cultivation is wasteful because land is left idle after a few seasons. Give one reason the Paharias might have had for the practice and say what evidence could test the officer's claim.

answer.model_answer_md: A patch cleared by burning could be sown for a few seasons and then **left while the forest grew back**, and the forest still gave other produce, so it was not simply idle. **Paharia accounts, and records of how soon patches were sown again and what they yielded,** could test the claim.

questions.stem_md: Explain three grievances that led the Santhals to rise in the hul of 1855–56.
questions.solution_md: Taxation, moneylenders and zamindars, three pressures on the Santhal settlers.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The state taxed the land they had cleared **heavily**. (2) **Moneylenders**, whom the Santhals called dikus, charged high interest and took their land when they could not repay. (3) **Zamindars** claimed control over the Damin area. Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the rising, which was suppressed.

questions.stem_md: The Paharias and the Santhals both lived in the Rajmahal region. Compare them in their way of living and in their dealings with the Company, and say what the contrast suggests about how the Company judged settled and hill peoples.
questions.solution_md: Comparison on three criteria, the contrast drawn and the limit of the evidence.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Livelihood:** the Paharias hunted, gathered forest produce and practised shifting cultivation; the Santhals cleared forest and settled to cultivate.
2. **Company policy:** the Company tried to crush the Paharias in the 1770s, then Cleveland paid chiefs allowances; the Santhals were encouraged to clear land and given the Damin-i-Koh in 1832.
3. **Outcomes:** the Paharias withdrew deeper into the hills; the Santhals spread but faced heavy tax, moneylenders and zamindars, and rose in the hul.
4. **Contrast:** the Company favoured settled revenue-paying cultivators and distrusted forest peoples, but this did not shield the Santhals.
5. **Caution:** our evidence is largely official.

questions.stem_md: In the ryotwari system of the Bombay Deccan, with whom was the land revenue settled?

options.text_md: A zamindar of each district
The ryot, the cultivator himself
The village moneylender
A merchant who exported cotton

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The ryot, the cultivator himself. Revenue was settled directly with each cultivator, with no zamindar in between.

questions.stem_md: Why did the demand for cotton from the Bombay Deccan rise sharply in the early 1860s?

options.text_md: The American Civil War cut off British mills from raw cotton grown in the United States
The Limitation Law of 1859 made loans cheaper for ryots
The ryotwari assessment was lowered in 1861
The Deccan Riots Commission asked ryots to grow more cotton

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The American Civil War cut off British mills from raw cotton grown in the United States. The war from 1861 to 1865 interrupted the usual supply to Britain. The other options name a law, a tax and a later inquiry that did not raise demand.

questions.stem_md: Historians link the Deccan cotton boom of the 1860s to the American Civil War. Which finding about an imagined Deccan district would most weaken that link?

options.text_md: Records showing that prices soared in 1862 and fell in 1866
Records showing that exporters' advances and cotton prices in the district were no higher in 1861–65 than in the years before the war
Records showing that exporters advanced money to sahukars, who lent it to ryots for cotton
Records showing that the area under cotton grew between 1861 and 1865

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Records showing that exporters' advances and cotton prices in the district were no higher in 1861–65 than in the years before the war. The link says the war raised demand and prices. If prices and advances did not rise in the war years, the link fails for that district; the other findings fit it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ryot's first bond was for 50 rupees. After three years with nothing paid he signed a second bond for 80 rupees, the unpaid interest having been added. At what yearly rate of simple interest on the 50 rupees did this happen?

options.text_md: 60 per cent a year
30 per cent a year
10 per cent a year
20 per cent a year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 20 per cent a year. The added interest is 30 rupees over three years, which is 10 rupees a year. Ten rupees is 20 per cent of 50. The figure of 60 per cent is the rate for the whole three years.

questions.stem_md: Why did Deccan sahukars make ryots sign new bonds every three years?

options.text_md: The law of 1859 gave a loan bond only three years of validity, so a fresh bond kept the debt enforceable
The ryotwari assessment was revised every three years
The Deccan Riots Commission had ordered it
Cotton prices were fixed for three years at a time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The law of 1859 gave a loan bond only three years of validity, so a fresh bond kept the debt enforceable. A bond that lapsed could not be enforced. Signing a new one before it lapsed kept the claim alive.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated page from a sahukar's account book notes that cotton prices are very high, that exporters are pressing him for more cotton and offering advances, and that he fears prices will collapse if peace returns across the ocean. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: After 1865, since prices are already collapsing
About 1875, the year of the riots
Between about 1861 and 1865, while the American war was still going on
Before 1857, since exporters were not yet looking to India for cotton

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Between about 1861 and 1865, while the American war was still going on. High prices, pressure from exporters and fear of peace overseas all fit the war years. Collapse is feared, not yet reported.

questions.stem_md: An imagined police report from May 1875 records that crowds in several villages of Poona and Ahmednagar districts demanded bonds and account books from sahukars and burnt them, but did not attack the government's offices. Which inference is the most careful?

options.text_md: The government's revenue demand had no part in the riots
The sahukars had broken the law of 1859 in every village
The crowds blamed the sahukars most directly, but the report alone cannot show that the revenue demand played no part in their distress
The riots had been planned by the police

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The crowds blamed the sahukars most directly, but the report alone cannot show that the revenue demand played no part in their distress. The targets show whom the crowds blamed. They do not show what else lay behind the distress, so claims about the revenue demand go beyond the report.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ryot's field was assessed at 12 rupees a year for thirty years. In the first year his crop sold for 40 rupees; in the fifteenth year the same crop sold for 24 rupees. Which statement follows?

options.text_md: The assessment took 30 per cent of the crop's value at first and 50 per cent after the fall, so an assessment fixed for long periods weighed more heavily when prices fell
The assessment took 30 per cent at first and 40 per cent later
The assessment fell with prices, so the burden stayed at 30 per cent
The ryot's burden was lighter in the fifteenth year, since the sum was the same

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The assessment took 30 per cent of the crop's value at first and 50 per cent after the fall, so an assessment fixed for long periods weighed more heavily when prices fell. Twelve of 40 is 30 per cent, and twelve of 24 is 50 per cent. A sum fixed in rupees does not fall when prices fall.

questions.stem_md: Explain two features of the ryotwari system in the Bombay Deccan that left ryots open to debt.
questions.solution_md: A high assessment fixed for long periods and its effect in bad years.

answer.model_answer_md: Revenue was assessed on the **expected average income** from each kind of soil and set at a **high level**. It was **revised only every thirty years**, so in bad years, such as the depression of the 1830s, ryots could not pay and many fled or fell into debt.

marking_scheme.step: Revision only every thirty years and effect in bad years

questions.stem_md: Explain how the American Civil War first helped and then hurt the cotton-growing ryots of the Bombay Deccan.
questions.solution_md: The boom, the end of the war and the debt that followed.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The war cut Britain's cotton from the United States, so demand for Indian cotton rose; exporters advanced money to sahukars, who lent to ryots, and **prices soared**. (2) When the war ended in **1865**, American cotton returned and demand for Indian cotton **fell**. (3) Credit dried up and ryots were left with **debts** they could not clear.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ryot borrows 200 rupees on a bond at 10 per cent a year, simple interest on the bond's principal, and pays nothing for six years. After three years the sahukar has him sign a new bond that adds the unpaid interest to the principal. (a) What does he owe after six years? (b) What would he owe if the 200 rupees had carried simple interest for six years with no new bond? (c) Why do the two sums differ?
questions.solution_md: Two sums computed and the reason for the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) After three years the interest is 60, so the new bond is 260; three more years at 10 per cent on 260 add 78, so he owes **338 rupees**. (b) Simple interest on 200 for six years is 120, giving **320 rupees**. (c) The difference of 18 rupees arises because the second bond charged interest on unpaid interest too.

questions.stem_md: Explain the causes of the Deccan riots of 1875, with reference to the ryotwari system, the cotton boom and the moneylenders.
questions.solution_md: The assessment, the boom and bust, the moneylenders' methods and the outbreak.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Ryotwari:** revenue was settled with each ryot at a high assessment, revised every thirty years, so ryots fell into debt, as in the 1830s.
2. **Cotton boom:** the American Civil War raised demand and prices; exporters advanced money through sahukars to ryots.
3. **Bust:** after 1865 demand fell, credit dried up and the debts remained.
4. **Moneylenders:** under the law of 1859 bonds lasted three years, so sahukars had new bonds signed, adding interest to principal and using other tricks.
5. **Outbreak:** in May 1875 ryots at Supa attacked sahukars, took their bonds and account books and burnt them; the revolt spread.

questions.stem_md: An imagined historian argues that the Deccan riots were caused by moneylenders' tricks and not by the revenue system of the government. Assess this argument, using the evidence of the bonds, the ryotwari assessment and the Deccan Riots Commission.
questions.solution_md: Evidence for the argument, evidence against, the commission's limits and a reasoned verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For:** crowds burnt bonds and account books and attacked sahukars, and the commission found anger against moneylenders and grain dealers.
2. **Tricks:** new bonds every three years, unpaid interest added to principal, no receipts and low prices for produce.
3. **Against:** the assessment was high and revised only every thirty years, so ryots had little to spare and were likely pushed to borrow.
4. **The commission:** set up by the government, it was reluctant to accept the revenue demand as a cause, so its silence is weak evidence.
5. **Judgement:** sahukars were the immediate target, but the demand probably deepened dependence on them; the argument is too narrow.

marking_scheme.step: The revenue demand as a further cause

An inquiry into riots in villages of the Deccan
A report to the British Parliament on the administration and activities of the Company in India, with long appendices

questions.stem_md: Two imagined accounts describe the same hill village. A surveyor's journal says the burnt patches were abandoned and wasted; a summary of the hill community's own songs says they were left to grow back and sown again. What is the best response for a historian?

Prefer the songs, since the community knew its land best
Reject both, since they disagree

**Assertion (A):** Two reports that give the same figure for estates auctioned in a district do not necessarily confirm it twice.

**Reason (R):** One of the reports may have copied the figure from the other, or both may have taken it from the same collector's return.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Agreement counts as confirmation only when the sources are independent, and copying removes that independence.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Historians treat official reports such as the Fifth Report as complete and neutral records of rural conditions.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Official reports are made for particular purposes and from particular viewpoints, so historians question what they leave out.

questions.stem_md: A collector's report says that the ryots of an estate were prosperous; an imagined petition from the same ryots says that they were in distress. State two things a historian should check before preferring either.
questions.solution_md: The writers' purposes, and independent records to test them.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Who wrote each and why**: a collector may wish to show good management, and ryots may stress distress to win relief. (2) **Other evidence from the same years**, such as rent registers, harvests and prices, to see which account fits the facts.

questions.stem_md: A student wants to describe how Deccan ryots experienced credit in the cotton years. She has the Deccan Riots Commission report, an imagined ryot's diary and an imagined sahukar's account book. Explain how she should use each and give one risk for each.
questions.solution_md: Each source matched to what it can show, with its risk.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The **commission's report** gives statements and statistics for many villages, but officials made it and may play down the revenue demand. (2) The **ryot's diary** shows how one family felt about debt, but it is one person's view and may lack figures. (3) The **sahukar's book** records loans and interest, but it is his own record and may leave out payments in grain.

questions.stem_md: An imagined historian wants to write about how the Company's revenue policies affected peasants in Bengal, the Rajmahal hills and the Deccan. She has the Fifth Report, Buchanan's journals and the Deccan Riots Commission report. Evaluate how far each serves her purpose and what else she needs.
questions.solution_md: Each report assessed for one region, the gaps and a framed conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Fifth Report (1813):** petitions, collectors' reports and revenue figures on Bengal; its critical aim may have exaggerated the decline of zamindari power.
2. **Buchanan's journals (1810–11):** a Company physician's observations of the hills; useful, but he judged the land as resources to be developed and criticised forest dwellers' ways.
3. **Commission report (1878):** statements and statistics on the Deccan, though reluctant to accept the revenue demand as a cause.
4. **Fit:** each suits one region best, and none gives peasants' own voices fully, so she needs district records, petitions and oral traditions.
5. **Judgement:** rich but official, so conclusions should be framed as readings of the Company's view.
